<reason>Both sides were excellent, but B built the stronger path. B's core move—separating the safety trigger from "basic terms" and grounding parity in species-specific exams (pork/trichinella, beef/BSE), truthful-disclosure labeling, and regulator reopening power—read the motion as written and absorbed nearly everything A threw at it. A's pressure answers were impressively direct (three post-approval rules unified by temporal hazards; published finish lines), and A landed real hits: the voluntary-vs-mandatory label distinction and the closing drift/template line. But A's own finish-line answer let B argue convergence with the motion's trigger, and A's remaining distinctions (drift verification, long-latency surveillance) were substantially answered by conventional analogues—ongoing product-specific testing and process-control verification already exist inside the conventional regime, and regulators added BSE requirements without abandoning parity. A's route required "same basic terms" to mean identical-in-substance terms, a reading the word "basic" cuts against; A's triviality counter was checked by B's live stakes (bans, impossible pathways, permanent second-class status). B's clipped opening is a small execution cost, not enough to offset the interpretive win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing jiu-jitsu ([B5.4]): A's answer to the "ban paid in installments" question—criteria published at approval with a clock—was reframed as simply specifying what "once safety standards are met" means, fulfilling the motion rather than defeating it, and B then argued A's three signature rules merely redescribed the existing meat regime. A's voluntary/mandatory label hit ([A4.4]) was the sharpest counter-punch, partially blunted by B's mandatory conventional-label examples (COOL, previously frozen).</best_rebuttal>
